This paper delves into the analysis of accretion variability observed in the near-infrared spectroscopic data of XX Cha, a 7.1 million year old T Tauri star located in the Chamaeleon I dark cloud. By examining the relationship between accretion rates and optical flux, we found that XX Cha exhibits a unique, non-linear dependence on this relationship when compared to other T Tauri stars. Furthermore, this non-linearity is evident across multiple spectroscopic indicators of accretion and optical flux. This non-linear behavior is thought to result from the variable geometry of the accretion disk, specifically the changing inclination of the disk as it evolves. This hypothesis is supported by the fact that XX Cha possesses a small inner disk extent, which is uncommon among T Tauri stars of similar age and mass. This assumption is based on historical observations of XX Cha, which showed a larger inner disk radius but is now disputed. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Evaluations using real-world 4G and 5G data demonstrate the scheme's efficacy. This model explores various design elements of the ancillary services market, including pricing mechanisms, supply incentives, and constraints, and their corresponding policy implications. This is demonstrated through an empirical analysis of German data from 2014 to 2019, which reveals the complex relationships between market variables and the duration of capacity reserves. The study's findings have important policy implications for market design, including the optimal pricing mechanism, supply constraints, and the effectiveness of incentives. By integrating the model with existing literature on electricity markets, it provides a foundation for further research into the effects of market interactions on the ancillary services market. This is particularly relevant for addressing the design challenges posed by the increasing penetration of renewable energy sources in the electricity sector. We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Notably, partial linearisation has a relationship with the Lie algebra of symplectic derivations, while the associated 2-form of a double vector bundle can be reconstructed using the Schouten-Nijenhuis bracket. This reveals that the image of the partial linearisation functor coincides with the category of symplectic double vector bundles. A new numerical method is being presented for simulating single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media using finite elements. This approach combines the use of continuous pressures and discrete fractures, with the fractures treated as straight segments and the pressure assumed to be constant along each fracture. This method meets the fundamental requirements for pressure continuity at the fracture-matrix interface, fulfills the balance equation in a weak sense within the fractures, and employs a suitable numerical upwinding technique to handle the high permeability of fractures. This results in a solvable algebraic problem with pressure continuity maintained at the fracture-matrix interfaces. This numerical method is proven to be stable and convergent, and it demonstrates better accuracy compared to a previous discrete fracture method. This is shown through the presentation of various test cases, including a complex geological model, which also highlights the de-pinning issue that this method avoids. This method is also more efficient than other approaches for solving flow problems within highly fractured media. This numerical method is then applied to a real-world example from the CO2 storage context. This approach can be implemented using existing finite element software, and it is available in the FEniCS framework under the DarcyFracture class. This includes examples of its usage. This numerical method can be adapted for use with other discretization techniques, such as finite differences. This paper also discusses the challenges associated with simulating flow within fractured media using hybrid methods within the Darcy flow context. This is the first part of a larger study that will also explore the development of a hybrid mixed finite element method for two-phase flow within fractured media. This will involve addressing the additional difficulties associated with two-phase flow, including phase separation within the fractures and the implementation of appropriate numerical upwinding techniques. The Bayes factor method is used to assess the reliability of hypotheses by comparing the likelihood of observed data given two competing models. This approach is particularly useful when comparing nonlinear statistical models. However, the bayes factor calculation is sensitive to certain issues that can render its effectiveness questionable. This talk will discuss two general techniques for addressing these issues: the use of default or robust prior distributions, and the application of Bayesian continuous reversible jump methods. These strategies are illustrated through analyses of two research studies: one examining the effects of exercise interventions and another studying the genetic causes of sleep disorders. These examples highlight the potential benefits of default and Bayesian reversible jump approaches in the context of Bayes factor calculations. Furthermore, the talk will address some of the common misconceptions surrounding Bayes factor methods, and provide guidance on how to conduct reliable analyses using R2jags. This includes discussions on the selection of prior distributions, the validation of Bayes factor estimates, and the assessment of model performance. Discourse markers like "however" and "in addition" facilitate the understanding of text relationships by indicating connections between sentences. To effectively train deep learning models for related tasks such as text classification, it's essential to analyze these connections. However, current methods often overlook the semantic roles played by discourse markers, which are a fundamental aspect of their meaning. To address this limitation, we developed a method to automatically extract the semantic roles of discourse markers from pre-existing resources. We utilized this information to enhance the performance of deep learning models in three classification benchmarks by incorporating the semantic roles of discourse markers into feature representations. Our results show that incorporating this information boosts performance by 4.5% on average. We open-sourced our framework, named DiscSense, to facilitate further research in this area.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We demonstrate that the geometry of the factorized space under the Riemannian quotient geometry aligns with these properties, which enables us to establish uniform bounds for key matrix norms and provides an efficient algorithm for matrix approximation, Burer-Monteiro style. We also show that the standard convex relaxation of this problem has a significant gap in terms of its Wasserstein distance from the Burer-Monteiro factorization. We numerically verify our theoretical findings using synthetic data generated randomly. We further apply this algorithm to the challenging problem of approximately solving a multivariate Gaussian mixture model, which yields promising results. We conclude by discussing possible connections to other optimization problems, including matrix completion, multiquadratic matrix estimation, and Gaussian mixture separation, which can be solved using this general algorithm. We make the code publicly available online. We end by suggesting several avenues for further research. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. A bipartite graph of a higher girth than 4 and a certain high degree, in this case a degree of 6, cannot be colored using the same number of colors mentioned in the original conjecture. A construction method for a cubic bipartite graph with a girth of 4 and edge coloring requirements that contradict the proposed limit is also presented. A modified version of the Petersen graph, a bipartite graph with a girth of 4 and a degree of 2, is used as the base for this construction. A different approach to represent the edge coloring condition as a vertex and edge labeling on the graph is also introduced. This new perspective allows for the use of the Collage Complexity, a measure of the computational difficulty of recognizing a concept, and the structure of the 4-gon to establish constraints on the vertex and edge labels. These constraints are then used to identify another cubic bipartite graph with a girth of 4 and a degree of 2, in this case the dual of the Barberton graph, which cannot be colored according to the proposed limit. This counterexample is a cubic bipartite graph with a girth of 4 and a degree of 2, that cannot be colored using 6 colors, but can be colored using 7 colors. Building on the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version is obtained by modifying the original twist using the $r$-twist operation, which involves a parameter $r$. This results in a family of Jordanian twists with a $q$-deformed analogue. Additionally, we have a twisted version of the $r$-twist operation, which leads to a subfamily of the Jordanian twists. These generalized Jordanian twists have $gl(2)$ as their underlying Lie algebra and have associated star products defined through their representation. The Poisson bracket and the $r$-twisted product of these forms can be expressed in terms of a differential operator, which has a singular point. This indicates that it belongs to a more general class of operator, which includes the conformally invariant operator as a specific case. Our proposed method, cluster-consistent word embedding for multiple languages in a single semantic space, addresses the challenge of integrating diverse linguistic structures into a unified framework without pre-existing monolingual models. We contend that leveraging intrinsic language properties, such as syntactic categories and lexical relationships, can facilitate the construction of a single semantic space that is applicable to multiple languages. Our approach utilizes a multi-task learning framework that combines intrinsic tasks like part-of-speech tagging and lexical clustering to train a single model capable of capturing both general semantic information and language-specific characteristics. We further introduce a cluster-consistent word embedding learning objective that ensures the embedding of different words that represent the same concept are positioned closely together, regardless of their linguistic affiliation. Our experiments on English, Spanish, French, and Chinese demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a multilingual setting, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in both intrinsic evaluation tasks and extrinsic downstream applications. We also explore the limitations of our approach by analyzing the results of integrating diverse languages with distinct typological characteristics, such as subject-object-verb order versus subject-verb-object order. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-hu/Multi-lingual-Word-Embedding.

Mobile agents require accurate navigation and mapping capabilities, and to meet this demand, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) has been developed to estimate positions and orientations using visual and inertial sensors. VIO algorithms using recurrent models have achieved high accuracy but often struggle with real-time performance due to increased computational costs. To address this challenge, a new External Memory Attention (EMA) VIO algorithm is proposed, leveraging external memory to store and manipulate past sensor readings and combine them with current information through attention mechanisms. This results in a lightweight and efficient model capable of handling large amounts of historical data. Experiments using the TUM-VIO and VIO-dataset benchmarks show that EMA-VIO outperforms a comparable recurrent VIO baseline in terms of accuracy and significantly reduces computational requirements. Furthermore, with a minimal increase in memory usage, this method can handle larger historical windows than the recurrent baseline. Source code for EMA-VIO is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the Weyl Hamiltonian, a pivotal concept in physics that describes certain exotic materials. By applying a modified transformation, we transform the Weyl Hamiltonian into a new form known as the square-root Weyl Hamiltonian or SRW, which defines a new material class - the square-root Weyl material. We identify three distinct types of SRW materials, analyze their unique properties, and demonstrate how they can be realized in two-dimensional and three-dimensional setups using graphene and platinum telluride as examples. Notably, the square-root Weyl materials exhibit distinct topological invariants and can serve as the starting point for multiple exotic states, offering guidance for experimental searches. This research paves the way for exploring the rich physics of square-root Weyl materials and related states. This work is also reflected in a companion paper titled "Square-root Dirac points in graphene". We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Furthermore, we show that the system's entropy also serves as a lower bound for the minimum time to release. Additionally, we explore the relationship between distinguishability time and various quantum system properties, demonstrating that it remains invariant under specific unitary transformations and providing upper and lower bounds in terms of various matrix norms and asymmetry measures. Lastly, we apply these findings to calculate the minimum time required to release a qubit in both the Landau-Zener problem and a driven damped Jaynes-Cummings model.

To address this issue, we present a cost-effective approach that reduces labeling costs for these models by limiting the annotation to just a small subset of text within specific regions of the documents, without the need to provide explicit bounding boxes or detailed labels for individual words. We call this approach "Partial Type Annotation" or PTA. To make PTA feasible, we developed a new model that can accurately infer the correct annotations for unseen documents. In extensive experiments, our model demonstrated significant improvements over existing methods when given only partial annotations. When evaluating our approach on real-world documents, we found that PTA can reduce labeling costs by as much as 87% while maintaining high accuracy in extracting relevant information. Our results also show that PTA can be a precursor to more advanced approaches like active learning, where the model selects specific regions of the documents that are most likely to confuse it, thus further decreasing labeling costs. An examination of 12 million Uber rides in Los Angeles and San Francisco before,
during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic reveals that riders' willingness to travel
to unfamiliar neighborhoods decreased significantly, with a 45% drop in one-month
newcomers in Los Angeles and a 25% drop in San Francisco.  This decline caused
commuting patterns to become more localized and less inclusive, leading to a
greater concentration of encounters among residents of the same income group.
In Los Angeles, income diversity in rides decreased by 12% and in San Francisco
by 8%.  These changes were more pronounced in areas already experiencing income
inequality, potentially exacerbating existing social divisions.  As people became
less mobile, their social networks expanded more slowly, with a 20-30% decrease
in the rate at which new friendships were formed.  These findings suggest that
social distancing measures may have unintentionally widened urban income gaps.

False news can lead to severe consequences in the political, economic, and social spheres, thereby posing a significant threat to individuals and society as a whole. Our approach employs a BERT-based model to generate potential labels, and we select the most likely label using the cosine similarity between the contextualized token embeddings. We apply this method to correct the annotations of emotion-related question types. Evaluations using a pre-trained set of parameters show that our approach enhances the consistency of annotated data, with a 12.67% reduction in type-consistency conflicts and a 10.83% increase in average annotation confidence. For mobile robots to effectively navigate unfamiliar surroundings, a strong mapping capability is essential. Current methods often rely on advanced SLAM techniques, but these can be resource-intensive and prone to failure in complex environments. A new, lightweight approach called HiTMap has been developed to address this challenge. This method creates a simplified map representation that focuses on a network of interconnected areas, using a graph structure to model the environment's topology. Each area is defined by a set of points of interest (POIs), which can be detected using features like corners and junctions. In HiTMap, areas are connected by edges that represent the relationships between local spaces, rather than precise path distances. This representation allows for efficient navigation using graph search algorithms, and can be updated incrementally as the robot explores its surroundings. The efficacy of this method has been demonstrated through simulation and real-world testing, with results showing HiTMap outperforms a basic grid-based mapping approach in terms of mapping size and navigation efficiency. The code for this project has been made available online.

As a superconductor's expelled field generates a parabolic gradient in the magnetic field, it can be made up of multiple spatially distinct components, each with a different wavelength that may be detectable up to a specific entanglement limit. This limit is determined by the balance between minimizing the curvature of the parabolic gradient to keep the expelled field within detectable ranges and maintaining the wavelength of atomic interference to its maximum possible value. This could be as high as 100 micrometers, allowing for the detection of very small superconducting samples. A proposed atomic interferometry system utilizing two hyperpump sequences in $^{87}$Rb atoms has an estimated entanglement limit of 0.3 nT in the $z$-direction, equivalent to a superconducting sample of 10 micrometers in diameter. This level of detection is on par with the most advanced atomic magnetometry systems. This approach offers a versatile method for exploring a wide range of phenomena related to the interplay of quantum states in materials science, including the behavior of vortices in superconductors and superfluids, and also provides a means to investigate the properties of superconducting materials in various quantum states. This would allow for the investigation of the minimal superconducting sizes achievable in various materials, potentially revealing the relationship between the size of the $d$-wave gap and the coherence length in cuprate superconductors. Our proposed memory allocator, DynaSOAr, streamlines memory management for object-oriented programming on GPUs by eliminating fragmentation and slowing cache coherence. DynaSOAr is an open-source allocator that is compatible with major compilers and can be easily integrated into existing projects. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, it shows that the number of those classes can be substantial, potentially even quadratic, and provides a lower estimate for the number of elements in the largest conjugacy class, which is now proven to be at least half the size of the group divided by its diameter squared. This achievement represents an improvement over a previous quadratic estimate from Breuillard and Tointon. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a group with a polynomial diameter can be expressed as the product of its largest conjugacy class, the second-largest conjugacy class, and a nilpotent subgroup of the lowest possible class, with a size that is directly calculable using the diameter and the number of elements in the two largest conjugacy classes. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using force and surface profile measurements and video recordings of liquid foam flow, this study demonstrates that surface roughness in a solid container causes variable-sized air pockets to form at the interface with a liquid foam, leading to increased frictional forces and surface profiles that vary over time. The study also reveals that the size of these air pockets is determined by the depth of container roughness and can be matched to sizes of bubbles in the foam, allowing for the identification of two modes of air pocket formation: where the size of the air pockets is greater than the bubble sizes and where they are similar in size. When the air pockets are larger than the bubbles, they can coalesce with the foam, contributing to increased flow resistance. In contrast, when the air pockets are similar in size to the bubbles, they can impede flow by creating obstacles that slow down the flow of foam. The increased resistance to flow caused by surface roughness may also apply to other complex liquids, such as emulsions and non-Newtonian fluids. The study highlights the importance of considering the interaction between rough surfaces and interfaces in the study of fluid dynamics. The findings related to air pockets that form at the interface between a solid surface and a liquid foam may have broader implications for the study of geological and biological flows, including the movement of fluids through porous media and the flow of bodily fluids within biological organisms. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the anomaly, we employed a strategy that detects and removes outlier samples, finding it essential for improving performance. The anomalous class was identified and excluded from the dataset. To tackle the classification task, a combination of transfer learning using convolutional neural networks was employed, yielding a 94.35% accuracy rate. Additionally, the effectiveness of various features was assessed using mutual information, with texture features demonstrating the highest discriminatory power. Furthermore, the influence of image preprocessing was explored, revealing that resizing images does not significantly impact performance. The code utilized in this study has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This study examines the behavior of an elastic membrane at the surface of a rotating Hele-Shaw cell as it is filled with a less dense fluid that is displaced by a more dense fluid. Similar to nonrotating scenarios, the membrane's instability takes the form of a pattern with a specific length that is influenced by the rate of rotation and the difference in fluid densities. As the rate of rotation increases, this pattern length decreases exponentially until it reaches a critical point where it suddenly increases exponentially. This change in pattern length is linked to a shift from a stable to an unstable state in a related but different, nonrotating scenario. This state transition can be anticipated when the rotation rate surpasses a certain point that is influenced by the curvature of the cell and the difference in fluid densities. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focus on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation often diverges from the desired output, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, we present a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that focuses on target word prediction by considering future words in the target sentence. This innovation allows our model to anticipate and adapt to complex relationships between source and target sentences. We evaluate our proposed model on publicly available data sets WMT16 for English to German, and WMT14 for English to Chinese, achieving significant improvements over the baseline. Furthermore, our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of BLEU score, demonstrating its effectiveness. Code for the model is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-liu/Look-Ahead-Attention.

Despite their effectiveness, the underlying principles of these networks remain obscure to many, hindering the development of new GCNN variants. This paper aims to demystify GCNNs by presenting a novel, intuitive analysis that leverages signal processing concepts, specifically matched filtering. We demonstrate how a fundamental GCNN component, the graph convolution operation, can be represented as a matched filtering process. By breaking down this process into its key components, we gain valuable insights into the GCNN convolution process, including the significance of spectral convolution, renormalization, and the role of the graph structure. These insights enable us to propose a new, simple variant of the GCNN convolution operation, the SpatialConv, that bypasses the use of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and other complex operations. In a set of experiments on commonly used datasets, SpatialConv proves to be a highly efficient variant of the standard GCNN convolution operation, outperforming existing optimized GCNN implementations while utilizing significantly fewer parameters. These results validate the effectiveness of the SpatialConv approach. The insights gained from our matched filtering analysis are applicable to a broader range of neural network structures that employ convolution operations in graph domains. The additional material includes a discussion on the limitations of the matched filtering approach, an examination of the relationship between the standard GCNN convolution operation and the SpatialConv variant, and an analysis of the impact of the graph structure on the performance of the SpatialConv variant. Elastography is an advanced imaging technique that provides the distribution of tissue mechanical properties by assessing tissue behavior under stress. Accurate estimation of elastography relies on precise calculation of tissue displacement during ultrasound scanning. In synthetic aperture ultrasound imaging, displacement estimation is particularly challenging due to the complex signal processing involved in the imaging method. A major issue with conventional synthetic aperture imaging is its limited ability to accurately measure lateral tissue displacement. Our research addresses this challenge by developing a novel synthetic aperture technique called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA). In VSSA, we generate a new synthetic aperture based on estimated lateral displacement, which significantly improves the displacement estimation accuracy in the imaging method. Our experimental results show that VSSA leads to a 3.5-fold reduction in displacement estimation error compared to conventional synthetic aperture imaging. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates the use of advanced displacement estimation algorithms such as the Total Fidelity Model, which results in a 2.5-fold improvement in estimation accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that VSSA outperforms conventional synthetic aperture imaging in various scenarios, thus it can be employed in a wide range of ultrasound elastography applications. Our research also highlights areas for further improvement, particularly in reducing VSSA's computational load. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/ali-gholami/VSSA. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach provides a new perspective on the relationship between algorithms and proofs and offers a method for converting existing algorithms into proofs. Furthermore, it enables the construction of algorithms from scratch, based on natural deductions and natural transformations, which can be achieved through a graphical interface called "Proof-to-Algorithm" (PtA). PtA allows users to generate algorithms from natural deductions by replacing deductions with procedure calls and replacing natural transformations with procedure compositions. This approach has been applied to develop algorithms for natural sorting and prefix matching, among others. This framework and its components are part of a broader research project aimed at exploring the relationship between algorithms and proofs, with the ultimate goal of developing methods for correcting and improving existing algorithms based on their underlying proofs. This research has been presented at ITP 2020 and FLoC WGP 2020. This paper includes an updated introduction, an expanded discussion on the context and related work, and an updated case study on natural sorting. It also introduces an improved version of PtA called "PtA 2.0" with enhanced features, including the ability to generate algorithms from natural deductions with variables and the ability to input algorithms as natural transformations. In the setting of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$, specifically $O(k \cdot d^{\log_{3}\gamma_{d}+1} + k\cdot\gamma_{d}^{k})$ dimensions, where $\gamma_{d}$ represents the minimum value in the distribution of Euclidean norms over a $d$-dimensional standard normal distribution. This storage improvement is significant as previous optimal solutions for this problem required a storage of $O(k \cdot d)$ dimensions. Furthermore, our algorithm provides an approximate solution with a clustering cost of $9$ times the optimal, which is an enhancement over the previous solution that offered a $6$ times the optimal clustering cost. The development of our algorithm is rooted in the binning method, which is an extension of the bucketing technique used in one-pass $k$-means clustering solutions for static data. The binning method is particularly valuable as it enables the creation of a coreset from a data stream without the need for storing individual points, offering a promising approach for addressing other similarity-based clustering problems in dynamic settings. The time complexity of our algorithm is $O(k \cdot d^{\log_{3}\gamma_{d}+1} + k\cdot\gamma_{d}^{k} \cdot d + d \cdot \Delta)$, which includes the cost of calculating the Euclidean distance between points and the time required for updating the coreset in response to data stream changes. The accuracy of our solution is guaranteed by the following result: the expected clustering cost of the coreset found in the final snapshot is no more than $9$ times the optimal cost of clustering the points in the last data stream snapshot, plus a small additive constant that depends on the distribution of Euclidean norms in the data. The development of our algorithm is accompanied by experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness on real-world and artificially generated data sets. The evaluation shows that our algorithm outperforms existing dynamic $k$-means clustering solutions in terms of storage capacity and clustering accuracy for a wide range of data sets. The evaluation also highlights the impact of various data set characteristics on the performance of our algorithm. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into subdomains and solving smaller versions of the game within each of them. A central controller then makes decisions at a higher level, utilizing the outcomes from these local domains to guide the subsequent actions of individual agents within them. Our research demonstrates that this hierarchical approach leads to significant reductions in computation time while achieving comparable levels of performance to optimally solving the original large-scale game. Our methodology is further enhanced by an efficient linear function approximation method for solving local subdomains, which enables us to tackle even more complex and larger-scale versions of the game. Our empirical evaluations show that this hierarchy can efficiently handle large-scale versions of the game with over 5000 states, making it an efficient tool for numerous real-world applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/strangsoft/hierarchical-pursuit-evasion. Our research also explores an existing linear hierarchical approach for reference purposes. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can significantly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Through a series of experiments with both
separate and shared dynamics models, we find that using distinct models for each
task can outperform a single, shared model when there is significant task
distinction. Furthermore, we observe that using separate models can reduce the
effect of negative knowledge transfer between tasks when there is little to no
distinction between them. This phenomenon is illustrated through an example
where using a single, shared model results in significant interference between
tasks, whereas separate models significantly reduce this interference. Our study
also explores various network architectures that can be used for separate models,
and finds that a simple, fully connected network can be beneficial when there
is little to no distinction between tasks. Finally, our study demonstrates how
using separate models can be an effective strategy for reducing negative
knowledge transfer between tasks, and provides a roadmap for future research in
this area. Our code is available online at: \url{https://github.com/abhinavc/mt-dril-saas}.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Building on this extension, we then prove the three balls theorem for functions that satisfy the Helmholtz decomposition within the R^n+1 space. Notably, this includes applications to the real and complex Hilbert spaces. Additionally, we establish that this theorem is viable for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator within these spaces. Furthermore, we explore its connection to the Rellich's theorem. Lastly, this paper also formulates the three balls theorem for the Dirac operator in the real and complex Hilbert spaces, providing a new mean to derive this theorem from the complex case. This is particularly significant as it breaks away from the conventional approach that relies on the maximum principle. This allows us to explore its implications for the Dirac operator in the real Hilbert space, providing a non-trivial alternative to the conventional proof based on the maximum principle. This paper's findings also reveal that the three balls theorem for the Dirac operator in the real Hilbert space can be derived from the complex Hilbert space using the Helmholtz decomposition, without relying on the Rellich's theorem. In solving inverse problems, researchers use generative adversarial networks (GANs) to reconstruct images by generating samples from a posterior distribution. A common issue with traditional methods is that training GANs requires a data augmentation process that isn't feasible in many real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, a conditional GAN is trained to produce a mean of the posterior distribution without using extra training data. A new regularized model, the conditional Wasserstein GAN (CWGAN), is proposed to improve the quality of generated samples. Experiments with a range of inverse problems show that the model outperforms the state-of-the-art in image reconstruction tasks. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems of fractional order and contrasts it with integer-order systems. Initially, a brief introduction to fractional-order systems, their stability analysis using the fractional equivalent of the center manifold theorem, and associated computations are provided. The article then delves into the details of this approach's limitations and the obstacles encountered in identifying invariant manifolds for fractional systems. The main challenge lies in the non-algebraic nature of the equilibrium point's stability conditions in fractional systems, which hinders the application of the implicit function theorem. As a result, invariant manifolds cannot be determined for these systems. The article also explores the relationship between the dimension of the global attractor and the dimension of the manifold in search of a counterpart to the Mandelbrot-James theorem for fractional systems. The article concludes by highlighting the difficulties in extending the center manifold theorem to higher-dimensional fractional systems and the potential benefits of alternative approaches, such as the numerical construction of invariant manifolds using radial basis functions. The article also includes an appendix detailing the computation of the monodromy matrix for fractional systems via the application of the Laplace transform to the state variables. The article ends by emphasizing the need for novel methods to analyze the stability of fractional systems, particularly those employing the attractivity criterion. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, shadows are shown to be compatible with tensor products over commutative ring objects, thereby providing a natural generalization of the concept of traces. This extension is demonstrated to yield a shadow for the THH of a bicategory equipped with a stratified cocycle, thereby generalizing the fundamental theorem of non-commutative motives to a broader, more inclusive context. parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and

can be empirically verified. Our model's structure also facilitates the use of
impulsivity-related averages and standard deviations as Tsallis parameters in
mathematical analyses of various phenomena. We demonstrate the applicability
of our model to the analysis of a specific scenario, namely the acceptance of
vaccination against COVID-19. Our model's success in this case highlights the
value of considering the standard deviation of delay discounting, which

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields an overdetermined second-order gauge theory.  However, when this gauge is applied to linearized massive gravity, a discrepancy arises due to the lack of a suitable set of harmonic gauge operators in certain mass-gravity scenarios, specifically in the Fierz-Pauli case and the Bouchendiane-Semeria (BS) model.  This issue can be circumvented by utilizing a modified harmonic gauge defined through a variation of the Euler-Lagrange approach, which results in a consistent harmonic gauge for these models.  Furthermore, this method reveals the presence of a new 'effective' harmonic gauge hidden within the Einstein-Hilbert action, specifically in the form of the BS action.  This approach can be extended to other gauge theories beyond massive gravity.  This note aims to provide a concise introduction to the harmonic gauge, discuss its application to the Einstein-Hilbert action, and examine the modified harmonic gauge within the context of mass-gravity theories.  This includes a detailed derivation of the harmonic gauge operators, as well as an exploration of the de Donder and harmonic gauge operators in relation to the Euler-Lagrange approach.  This work also touches on the hidden nature of the harmonic gauge in the Einstein-Hilbert action and the BS action, and concludes by discussing possible avenues for further research into the properties of the harmonic gauge within gauge theories.
